record.original_question: Does every complete Riemannian manifold with finite volume have at least one closed geodesic?

evidence.quote: Does every complete Riemannian manifold with finite volume have at least one closed geodesic?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,g)$ be a complete Riemannian manifold (without boundary) such that the Riemannian volume of $M$ with respect to $g$ is finite. A closed geodesic is a non-constant smooth map $\gamma:S^1\to M$ that is a geodesic of $(M,g)$, i.e., a periodic geodesic of positive length.

Question: Must $(M,g)$ admit at least one closed geodesic?
artifact.status_search_result: The question (attributed to Bangert) is known to have an affirmative answer in dimension 2, where complete finite-volume Riemannian surfaces are known to carry even infinitely many geometrically distinct closed geodesics. In dimensions 3 and higher the problem is still open: the standard Birkhoff minimax arguments used in dimension 2 do not extend, and no general existence result is known.

status_evidence.title: Open Problems and Questions about Geodesics — Burns and Matveev
status_evidence.snippet: Does every complete Riemannian manifold with finite volume have at least one closed geodesic? ... The question is solved in dimension 2 ... The argument is based on the Birkhoff minimax procedure and does not work in dimensions ≥ 3.
status_evidence.claim: Problem is open in dimension ≥ 3 and solved (with infinitely many closed geodesics) in dimension 2.

status_evidence.title: On the existence of infinitely many closed geodesics on non-compact manifolds
status_evidence.snippet: existence of closed geodesics on non-compact Riemannian manifolds of finite volume
status_evidence.claim: Active research direction; existence in higher dimensions remains an open question in general.
